title: Ordered gaps versus distance gaps
subtitle: G2 lecture 031000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Expanded companion deck developed from the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix. Adds explicit mathematical formulas, worked examples, and topic-specific diagrams while remaining standalone.

slides.title: Two notions of separation
slides.lead: Later bounds depend not merely on how far two spectral sets are apart, but on how they are ordered.
body: If two subsets of the real line are disjoint, their distance may be positive. But a stronger situation occurs when every point of one set lies to the left of every point of the other. That is ordered separation.
For self-adjoint spectral problems, this stronger geometry interacts well with quadratic forms and with the Sylvester equation that appears in Davis–Kahan.
slides.takeaway: Disjointness is enough for some statements; an ordered gap supports stronger estimates.

slides.title: Distance gap on the number line
slides.lead: The distance gap measures the closest approach of the two sets.
body: This quantity is symmetric: swapping S and T changes nothing. It only asks for geometric separation, not which set lies to the left or right.
A positive distance gap is already enough to guarantee invertibility for several operator constructions. But it does not encode directional information.
slides.takeaway: The distance gap is an unsigned separation quantity.

slides.title: Ordered gap adds orientation
slides.lead: When one set lies completely to the left of the other, we can measure the gap with a sign convention built into the order.
slides.mathtex: \delta_{\mathrm{ord}}(S,T)=\inf\{t-s:s\in S,\ t\in T\}\quad\text{when } s\le t\ \text{for all } s\in S,t\in T
body: This definition makes sense only when S is entirely to the left of T. In that case the quantity is positive precisely when the two sets are separated by a nonzero interval.
Ordered gaps break symmetry on purpose. The left-right arrangement matches the sign structure in several later quadratic-form arguments.
slides.takeaway: Ordered separation is a stronger hypothesis because it remembers who is left and who is right.

slides.title: Internal, external, and mixed gaps
slides.lead: A selected spectral cluster can have several different neighbors, so we must say what is being separated from what.
body: An internal gap measures spacing between eigenvalues inside the selected cluster. An external gap measures distance from the cluster to the rest of the spectrum. A mixed gap compares one specific part of the cluster to one specific part of the complement.

Davis–Kahan uses external separation: the selected subspace is compared with the complementary spectral region. Internal spacing may matter for numerical interpretation, but it is not the same hypothesis.
slides.takeaway: Always identify the two sets being separated before quoting a gap bound.

slides.title: Translating the picture to operators
slides.lead: Choose a spectral projector P for the selected cluster and split the Hilbert space into its range and complement.
body: Relative to H = ran P ⊕ ran P^⊥, a self-adjoint operator becomes a block matrix. The diagonal blocks carry the “inside” and “outside” spectra, while an off-diagonal perturbation couples them.
The spectral sets appearing in the gap condition are therefore spectra of block restrictions, not arbitrary numbers floating on a line. The separation hypothesis belongs to this block decomposition.
slides.takeaway: Gap assumptions are statements about spectra of the diagonal blocks determined by the chosen projector.

slides.title: Why the scalar model matters
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 031000 · A scalar preview of Sylvester
slides.lead: The operator equation AX − XB = C is already visible in the scalar identity (a − b)x = c.
body: If a and b are separated, the denominator stays away from zero and x is controlled by c divided by the gap. In the operator setting, the same logic survives through the Sylvester equation.
Ordered separation is especially convenient when a and b come from left and right spectral blocks of a self-adjoint operator, because then quadratic forms can preserve the sign of b − a.
slides.takeaway: A spectral gap appears later as the denominator that stabilizes the Sylvester solution.

slides.title: Ordered gaps feed quadratic-form bounds
slides.lead: Self-adjoint operators allow us to test inequalities on vectors rather than only on norms.
body: Suppose one block has spectrum in (−∞, α] and the other in [β, ∞) with α < β. Then every vector in the left block sees quadratic form values at most α‖x‖², while every vector in the right block sees values at least β‖x‖².

Subtracting these inequalities produces a uniform lower bound by β − α. That argument needs the ordered location of the spectra; an unsigned distance alone does not supply the same one-sided inequalities.
slides.takeaway: Ordered gaps convert spectral placement into one-sided quadratic-form estimates.

slides.title: Distance-only separation can be enough elsewhere
slides.lead: Not every theorem needs the extra structure of left-versus-right placement.
body: For general Banach-space Sylvester theory, disjoint spectra with positive distance are often enough. There, one proves invertibility by contour integrals, semigroup representations, or resolvent estimates that treat the two sets symmetrically.
But when we want clean self-adjoint inequalities and direct links to principal-angle bounds, ordered gaps usually produce the sharper or more transparent statement.
slides.takeaway: Distance separation is more general; ordered separation is more structured.

slides.title: A diagnostic question
slides.lead: Before using a gap theorem, identify which kind of separation the theorem actually assumes.
body: Ask three questions. Which spectral set corresponds to the selected subspace? Which set corresponds to the complement or comparison block? And does the theorem require only positive distance, or the stronger hypothesis that one set lies entirely to one side of the other?
This habit prevents a common mistake: reading an ordered-gap theorem as though any disjoint spectral sets satisfied it.
slides.takeaway: Never quote “the gap” without specifying both the sets and the kind of separation.

slides.title: What to remember
slides.lead: The numerical size of a gap and the geometric form of the separation are both part of the hypothesis.
body: Distance gaps say the sets are apart. Ordered gaps say one lies uniformly to the left of the other. The second statement is stronger, asymmetric, and tailored to self-adjoint block arguments.
This distinction will recur whenever we solve Sylvester equations or turn spectral placement into subspace-angle estimates. It is part of the theorem statement, not an afterthought.
slides.takeaway: Ordered gaps are a specialized but powerful upgrade of plain spectral distance.
